title: Judges 18:27–31
context: The Danites strike Laish, a quiet and unsuspecting people, rebuild it, and rename it Dan. They set up Micah’s image, served by Jonathan son of Gershom son of Moses and his descendants until the captivity of the land, while God’s house stood at Shiloh. The story explains the origin of a long-lasting rival sanctuary in the north.

verses.text: They took that which Micah had made, and the priest whom he had, and came to Laish, to a people quiet and unsuspecting, and struck them with the edge of the sword; then they burned the city with fire.
verses.arminianNotes: The Danites strike Laish, a quiet and unsuspecting people, and burn the city. Arminian readers stress the narrator’s repeated description of the people as peaceful, which invites readers to feel the injustice of the attack.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator reports no word from God commanding the attack and records the conquest without approval, leaving readers to weigh it against the law and the refrain of the epilogue.

verses.text: There was no deliverer, because it was far from Sidon, and they had no dealings with anyone else; and it was in the valley that lies by Beth Rehob. They built the city and lived in it.
verses.arminianNotes: No deliverer came because Laish was isolated. Arminian readers note the vulnerability of the defenseless and the absence of anyone to help, a theme of the whole epilogue.
verses.reformedNotes: The valley near Beth Rehob locates the city in the far north (compare Numbers 13:21). Reformed readers note that the Danites rebuild and settle, but on a foundation of violence and stolen worship.

verses.text: They called the name of the city Dan, after the name of Dan their father, who was born to Israel; however the name of the city used to be Laish.
verses.arminianNotes: They name the city Dan after their ancestor. Arminian readers see a tribe establishing its identity, though the name now carries the memory of how the city was taken.
verses.reformedNotes: Joshua 19:47 records the same renaming of Leshem, generally taken as another name for Laish. Reformed readers note that the place later became a center of false worship under Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:29-30).

verses.text: The children of Dan set up for themselves the engraved image; and Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Moses, and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day of the captivity of the land.
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan son of Gershom son of Moses becomes priest of the Danite shrine. Arminian readers find it striking that a descendant of Moses serves an idol, a reminder that faith is not inherited automatically.
verses.reformedNotes: Son may mean descendant, so Jonathan could be a later member of Moses’ line. Interpreters debate whether the captivity of the land refers to the Assyrian deportations or an earlier disaster; Reformed readers generally leave the dating open.

verses.text: So they set up for themselves Micah’s engraved image which he made, and it remained all the time that God’s house was in Shiloh.
verses.arminianNotes: The image remained as long as God’s house was in Shiloh. Arminian readers note the contrast between the true sanctuary and the rival shrine, which existed side by side for a long time.
verses.reformedNotes: Shiloh, where the tabernacle was set up in Joshua 18:1, stands as the legitimate center of worship. Reformed readers see the narrator’s closing note as an indictment of worship that ignored God’s chosen place.
